The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. Second, the series cover the civilian economy as reported to the republican statistical office. Military production, organised through all-Union enterprises and never reported at the republican level, is not captured, and Latvia hosted more of it than its neighbours: the VEF electrotechnical works, the Riga radio and instrument plants and the shipyards all carried `special' production for the Soviet armed forces \parencites[59--61]{upmalis_2015_latvijas}[74--5]{blaubergs_2015_vef}[103--4]{wbtransitionlatv}; the size of the Soviet garrison is likewise unknown between 1941 and 1989 and is treated as a source of bias below. The fuel index for 1980--90 is taken from the World Bank's study and extended with peat and natural gas; where a product series begins or ends with zero, production is assumed absent in the adjacent years. The branches are combined with the branch structure of the 1990 benchmark. The Soviet-period trade index instead chains the retail and wholesale turnover indices at comparable prices compiled by the Soviet statistical offices, the early post-war years coming from the USSR domestic-trade compendia; these are the only value series in the reconstruction. Finance and insurance follow employment, adjusted for productivity with the ratio of trade turnover to trade employment, as the CIA did; housing follows the housing stock derived from construction and population \parencites[319]{Maddison1998b}[49]{cia1982a}. \textit{Public and other services.} Public administration, health, education and science follow employment by branch, as in the CIA's accounts, with gaps in 1941--4, 1946--9 and 1951--4 interpolated. Defence is the least secure component. The Soviet garrison admitted under the mutual-assistance pact of October 1939 numbered about 30,000 \parencite[15--16]{years_of_dependence}, and some 80,000 Soviet troops were stationed in Latvia in 1990, far more in proportion to population than in Lithuania or Estonia; between those dates the garrison is interpolated between the 1940 and 1990 totals in step with public-administration employment, and after 1990 the index follows the withdrawal schedule and the formation of the Latvian forces. \textit{The war years.} Latvia was under German civil administration from 1941 to 1944, and the \textit{Reichskommissariat Ostland} published statistics, the \textit{Statistische Berichte für das Ostland} of 1942--4 and \textit{Ostland in Zahlen}, that cover crops, livestock, industrial output and employment but little else. The series to 1944 refer to the borders of the republic and the series from 1945 to present-day borders. This is the convention of the Maddison Project, which treats income per head as unaffected by a territorial change that moves less than a third of the population \parencites[629]{maddison_project_paper2014}[30]{bolt_zanden_newgdp2021}; the transferred district held a few per cent of the pre-war population at most \parencites[74]{years_of_dependence}[129--30]{hiden_salmon}, and was rural and poorer than the national average, so that the break in income per head is small and no adjustment has been made. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The parities, by sector of origin, were 0.40 dollars per rouble in agriculture, 1.80 in industry, 1.10 in construction, 2.80 in transport, 1.45 in trade and 3.30 in other services, or 1.82 for GDP as a whole \parencite[181, 184]{bolotin1992}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. Bolotin started from the republican GDP totals for 1990 compiled by Goskomstat in 1990--1, 1990 being one of the first years for which republican accounts on an SNA-type definition were compiled \parencite[43--4]{gulans_2015_rupnieciba} and the first with purchasing-power parities, and converted them into dollars with parities estimated, as he put it, `in practically full conformity' with the International Comparison Project. The parities, by sector of origin, were 0.40 dollars per rouble in agriculture, 1.80 in industry, 1.10 in construction, 2.80 in transport, 1.45 in trade and 3.30 in other services, or 1.82 for GDP as a whole \parencite[181, 184]{bolotin1992}. For Latvia the result is \lv{1990}~\intlnineteen{} per head, between Lithuania's 7,475 and Estonia's 8,425. Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks} shows the sectoral composition in roubles, with services other than trade and transport allocated by the 1987 Soviet input--output table \parencite{wbinputoutput1987}, beside the 1935 benchmark of \textcite{norkuslatvia1935} on which the interwar series rests. The rouble shares are domestic-price weights, like the lats shares of 1935, and are the weights with which the volume indices are combined; the dollar conversion applies to the total alone. They are at the market prices of 1990, so that product taxes and subsidies are carried within the sectors that bore them; no re-pricing to adjusted factor cost was attempted, since no republican data on the incidence of net product taxes by branch exist, and the only socialist economies for which the World Bank reports the ratio of product taxes less subsidies to value-added, Bulgaria and Ukraine in 1980--90, show about 0.5 per cent \parencite{wdi2024}.\footnote{The turnover tax, the principal product tax, was levied on final consumption goods and accrued to the republic where the finished good was made, as with cotton fabric woven in the Baltics from cheaply procured Uzbek cotton \parencite[20]{yasin_1993_economic}.} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T1_benchmarks.tex} Three features of the benchmark need stating, because the reconstruction stands or falls with it. First, its level is conservative. Bolotin's figure for the Soviet Union as a whole, 6,275~\intlnineteen{} per head, lies below Maddison's own estimate for 1987, and the bilateral Austria--USSR comparison on which it draws placed the Union at 32 per cent of the United States where the CIA had placed it at 42 per cent \parencite[318--19]{Maddison1998b}. Maddison nevertheless built the Maddison Project's 1990 levels for the republics from Bolotin's republic-to-Union ratios of 1991 rather than 1990, ratios inflated by the first year of transition, and then carried them backwards with net material product growth \parencite[181--2]{maddisonworldeconomy}; the consequences for Latvia are shown in Table~\ref{tab:previous} below. Second, the parities are Union-wide, so that the conversion assumes that relative prices in Latvia were those of the Soviet Union as a whole. For the material sectors this is a reasonable approximation in a planned economy with administered prices; for services, where the parity of 3.30 dollars per rouble reflects the very low rouble wages of the non-market sector, it is less certain, and the resulting share of services in Latvian GDP at rouble prices, 47 per cent, is above the 34 per cent implied by the World Bank's 1990 sectoral data \parencite{wbstatisticalhandbook1994}; the sensitivity of the series to this allocation is examined below. Third, there is no alternative.\footnote{Earlier claims ranged widely: PlanEcon's CIA-based estimate for Estonia in 1989 was 6,240 dollars against 5,000 for the Union \parencite[166]{kukk2005}.} Ponomarenko's accounts cover Russia alone and make no dollar conversion; the World Bank's GDP levels for 1980--91 were discontinued; the UNECE's `real GDP' indices for 1980--90 were taken from net material product, and the early Total Economy Database reproduced them \parencites{wbtransitionlatv}[32--3]{worldtables1995}[249]{UNECE1995}; the CIA's 1982 benchmark cannot be decomposed by republic, and the 1987 input--output table understates services too severely to serve as a benchmark \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. Second, the parities are Union-wide, so that the conversion assumes that relative prices in Latvia were those of the Soviet Union as a whole. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. For the material sectors this is a reasonable approximation in a planned economy with administered prices; for services, where the parity of 3.30 dollars per rouble reflects the very low rouble wages of the non-market sector, it is less certain, and the resulting share of services in Latvian GDP at rouble prices, 47 per cent, is above the 34 per cent implied by the World Bank's 1990 sectoral data \parencite{wbstatisticalhandbook1994}; the sensitivity of the series to this allocation is examined below. Third, there is no alternative.\footnote{Earlier claims ranged widely: PlanEcon's CIA-based estimate for Estonia in 1989 was 6,240 dollars against 5,000 for the Union \parencite[166]{kukk2005}.} Ponomarenko's accounts cover Russia alone and make no dollar conversion; the World Bank's GDP levels for 1980--91 were discontinued; the UNECE's `real GDP' indices for 1980--90 were taken from net material product, and the early Total Economy Database reproduced them \parencites{wbtransitionlatv}[32--3]{worldtables1995}[249]{UNECE1995}; the CIA's 1982 benchmark cannot be decomposed by republic, and the 1987 input--output table understates services too severely to serve as a benchmark \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. The choice of 1990 means that the series is extrapolated backwards for more than fifty years from end-of-period weights. The practical reason is that 1990 is the only year for which republican accounts on an SNA definition and purchasing-power parities exist together. Two further considerations favour it: the reporting of 1989--90, at the height of glasnost, was more transparent than that of any earlier Soviet year, the manipulation of earlier returns having been publicly acknowledged by Baltic statisticians in 1988 \parencite{adlys1988}; and 1990 is a year in which the branches that barely existed in 1940, electrical engineering, chemicals, pharmaceuticals or microbus production, can be observed and weighted at all \parencites[278]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1950}[303, 305]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1960}. The cost is that half a century is valued at end-period relative prices, which, as the sensitivity analysis explains, tends to understate growth; the short answer is that the consequence can be tested directly, because the Soviet-period series meets an independent series with 1935 weights in 1937--40. \subsection{Volume indices and their sources} Table~\ref{tab:sources} summarises the indicators and sources for each sector; the online appendix documents every series year by year. The Soviet-period indices are built from the statistical yearbooks of the Latvian SSR, which from 1957 give annual physical output from the mid-1950s and, unusually among the Baltic republics, cover the early post-war years, though incompletely; from the statistical bulletins published by the German civil administration for 1942--4; from the USSR compendia on domestic trade and on the national economy; from the World Bank's studies of 1993--6; and from archival material, notably the returns of the Latvian statistical administration on sown areas for 1945--55 and the transport returns of 1945--50 held in the Russian State Archive of the Economy. Three general points precede the detail. First, archival material is used to fill the early post-war years that the yearbooks cover incompletely, not merely to decorate the series; but, unlike for Lithuania and Estonia, no archival compilation of late-1980s output values at the product level could be found for Latvia, so that the 129 product series are consolidated into 22 minor branches by averaging and the minor branches weighted with the 1987 input--output study and the World Bank's 1993 valuation \parencites[82--5]{wbinputoutput1987}[289]{wbtransitionlatv}. Second, the series cover the civilian economy as reported to the republican statistical office. Military production, organised through all-Union enterprises and never reported at the republican level, is not captured, and Latvia hosted more of it than its neighbours: the VEF electrotechnical works, the Riga radio and instrument plants and the shipyards all carried `special' production for the Soviet armed forces \parencites[59--61]{upmalis_2015_latvijas}[74--5]{blaubergs_2015_vef}[103--4]{wbtransitionlatv}; the size of the Soviet garrison is likewise unknown between 1941 and 1989 and is treated as a source of bias below. Third, the year 1944 proved beyond reconstruction from Latvian sources, so that sectoral movements for 1943--5 are taken from the ratios observed in Lithuania, where documentation is better. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T2_sources.tex} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T2b_products.tex} \textit{Agriculture, forestry and fishing.} The index combines physical output of nine to ten crop categories and seven to sixteen animal products with timber removals and the fish catch, each sub-index weighted by its 1990 value-added, the crop and livestock weights coming from the World Bank's 1993 study and the split within grains from the Eurostat agricultural accounts \parencite[286]{wbtransitionlatv}. Early post-war output comes from unpublished returns on sown areas; yields for 1941--9 are obtained from animal numbers and the yields per animal of 1940, 1945 and 1950; disaggregated grain data for 1947--52 are not available, so that the grain categories move with the total. \textit{Industry.} Physical output series could be assembled for 129 products in ten of the eleven branches of the benchmark, electricity, fuels, metals, chemicals, machine-building and metal-working, wood and paper, building materials, light industry, food and a residual; the eleventh, petroleum refining, did not exist in Latvia (Table~\ref{tab:products}). The fuel index for 1980--90 is taken from the World Bank's study and extended with peat and natural gas; where a product series begins or ends with zero, production is assumed absent in the adjacent years. The branches are combined with the branch structure of the 1990 benchmark. For the interwar years the published manufacturing volume index for 1930--9 is used and the earlier years rest on employment adjusted for real wages, as in the Lithuanian and Estonian series \parencite[39, 45]{ostlandinzahlen}. \textit{Construction.} The Soviet-period index is a weighted index of the material inputs into construction, with weights from the 1987 input--output table, which is the CIA's procedure \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. \textit{Transport and communications.} Freight tonne-kilometres and passenger-kilometres across all modes are combined with a communications index built from postal and telegraph traffic, long-distance calls and radio and television sets in use, with weights from the 1987 input--output study. The years 1945--50 come from the Russian State Archive of the Economy; for 1941--4 no transport data exist and the sector is assumed to move with the rest of the economy; after 1990 the index follows sectoral employment. \textit{Trade, finance and housing.} Under planning industrial products circulated by allocation rather than through markets, so that the marketed-share approach of the interwar series cannot be used. The Soviet-period trade index instead chains the retail and wholesale turnover indices at comparable prices compiled by the Soviet statistical offices, the early post-war years coming from the USSR domestic-trade compendia; these are the only value series in the reconstruction. Finance and insurance follow employment, adjusted for productivity with the ratio of trade turnover to trade employment, as the CIA did; housing follows the housing stock derived from construction and population \parencites[319]{Maddison1998b}[49]{cia1982a}. \textit{Public and other services.} Public administration, health, education and science follow employment by branch, as in the CIA's accounts, with gaps in 1941--4, 1946--9 and 1951--4 interpolated. The Soviet garrison admitted under the mutual-assistance pact of October 1939 numbered about 30,000 \parencite[15--16]{years_of_dependence}, and some 80,000 Soviet troops were stationed in Latvia in 1990, far more in proportion to population than in Lithuania or Estonia; between those dates the garrison is interpolated between the 1940 and 1990 totals in step with public-administration employment, and after 1990 the index follows the withdrawal schedule and the formation of the Latvian forces. \textit{The war years.} Latvia was under German civil administration from 1941 to 1944, and the \textit{Reichskommissariat Ostland} published statistics, the \textit{Statistische Berichte für das Ostland} of 1942--4 and \textit{Ostland in Zahlen}, that cover crops, livestock, industrial output and employment but little else. The series to 1944 refer to the borders of the republic and the series from 1945 to present-day borders. This is the convention of the Maddison Project, which treats income per head as unaffected by a territorial change that moves less than a third of the population \parencites[629]{maddison_project_paper2014}[30]{bolt_zanden_newgdp2021}; the transferred district held a few per cent of the pre-war population at most \parencites[74]{years_of_dependence}[129--30]{hiden_salmon}, and was rural and poorer than the national average, so that the break in income per head is small and no adjustment has been made. The test is demanding. The two series share no sources, the one resting on the republic's own statistics and the other on Soviet yearbooks and post-war archives; no weights, one using the structure of 1935 and the other that of 1990; and no benchmark, one a bilateral price comparison with Sweden, the other a purchasing-power-parity study of the Soviet republics fifty-five years later. The first is the index-number problem of a single late benchmark. A late base assigns to each sector the relative prices of the end of the period, and since the sectors that grew fastest were those whose relative prices fell, late weights understate growth; this is the effect that Gerschenkron showed for Soviet machinery, when Bergson's GNP for 1928--37 grows by 175 per cent at 1928 prices and by 62 per cent at 1937 prices \parencites[453]{gerschenkron1957}[517]{feinsteinthomas2002}. The effect is concentrated in the early phases of industrialisation \parencite[85]{jonassardy1970}, and for the post-war Soviet economy it is modest: the CIA's move from 1970 to 1982 prices lowered measured growth over 1951--84 by about half a point a year \parencites[8]{cia1990}[156]{harrison1993}. The bound comes from the data: if 1990 weights understated Latvian growth over 1940--90, the Soviet-period series would arrive in 1937--40 systematically above the 1935-weighted interwar series, and it does not. And the procedure is that of every comparable reconstruction, the CIA's 1982 weights for 1950--90 among them, in which Maddison found `nothing untoward' \parencite[312]{Maddison1998b}. The second is the fixed ratio of value-added to gross output. Thomas and Feinstein's simulations found that the procedure understated value-added growth by between 0.15 and 1 percentage point a year; the Swedish accounts, which allow single- and double-deflated series to be compared, show an understatement of the deflator of 17 per cent over the three-quarters of a century after 1875 \parencites[19]{swedengdp_15602010}[148--53]{lobellschonkrantz2008}, and the bound in Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}, 14 per cent over the half-century, is in the lower part of that range, as befits indices that track output product by product and an economy that adhered to mass-production methods throughout its existence \parencite[195--7]{berend_centraleastern19441993}. The sign of the bias depends on the movement of input relative to output prices, and the Swedish figure is taken as a bound on its magnitude rather than as evidence of its direction in a planned economy. The error accumulates over the extrapolation and is largest in the earliest years of the Soviet-period series, precisely where the overlap shows the series within 3.5 per cent of an independent level. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The cost is that half a century is valued at end-period relative prices, which, as the sensitivity analysis explains, tends to understate growth; the short answer is that the consequence can be tested directly, because the Soviet-period series meets an independent series with 1935 weights in 1937--40. \subsection{Volume indices and their sources} Table~\ref{tab:sources} summarises the indicators and sources for each sector; the online appendix documents every series year by year. The Soviet-period indices are built from the statistical yearbooks of the Latvian SSR, which from 1957 give annual physical output from the mid-1950s and, unusually among the Baltic republics, cover the early post-war years, though incompletely; from the statistical bulletins published by the German civil administration for 1942--4; from the USSR compendia on domestic trade and on the national economy; from the World Bank's studies of 1993--6; and from archival material, notably the returns of the Latvian statistical administration on sown areas for 1945--55 and the transport returns of 1945--50 held in the Russian State Archive of the Economy. Three general points precede the detail. First, archival material is used to fill the early post-war years that the yearbooks cover incompletely, not merely to decorate the series; but, unlike for Lithuania and Estonia, no archival compilation of late-1980s output values at the product level could be found for Latvia, so that the 129 product series are consolidated into 22 minor branches by averaging and the minor branches weighted with the 1987 input--output study and the World Bank's 1993 valuation \parencites[82--5]{wbinputoutput1987}[289]{wbtransitionlatv}. Second, the series cover the civilian economy as reported to the republican statistical office. Military production, organised through all-Union enterprises and never reported at the republican level, is not captured, and Latvia hosted more of it than its neighbours: the VEF electrotechnical works, the Riga radio and instrument plants and the shipyards all carried `special' production for the Soviet armed forces \parencites[59--61]{upmalis_2015_latvijas}[74--5]{blaubergs_2015_vef}[103--4]{wbtransitionlatv}; the size of the Soviet garrison is likewise unknown between 1941 and 1989 and is treated as a source of bias below. The fuel index for 1980--90 is taken from the World Bank's study and extended with peat and natural gas; where a product series begins or ends with zero, production is assumed absent in the adjacent years. The branches are combined with the branch structure of the 1990 benchmark. The Soviet-period trade index instead chains the retail and wholesale turnover indices at comparable prices compiled by the Soviet statistical offices, the early post-war years coming from the USSR domestic-trade compendia; these are the only value series in the reconstruction. The Soviet garrison admitted under the mutual-assistance pact of October 1939 numbered about 30,000 \parencite[15--16]{years_of_dependence}, and some 80,000 Soviet troops were stationed in Latvia in 1990, far more in proportion to population than in Lithuania or Estonia; between those dates the garrison is interpolated between the 1940 and 1990 totals in step with public-administration employment, and after 1990 the index follows the withdrawal schedule and the formation of the Latvian forces. \textit{The war years.} Latvia was under German civil administration from 1941 to 1944, and the \textit{Reichskommissariat Ostland} published statistics, the \textit{Statistische Berichte für das Ostland} of 1942--4 and \textit{Ostland in Zahlen}, that cover crops, livestock, industrial output and employment but little else. Where these fail, the service sectors are interpolated between 1940 and the first post-war observation, and the movement between 1943 and 1945 is taken from the Lithuanian ratios. The test is demanding. The two series share no sources, the one resting on the republic's own statistics and the other on Soviet yearbooks and post-war archives; no weights, one using the structure of 1935 and the other that of 1990; and no benchmark, one a bilateral price comparison with Sweden, the other a purchasing-power-parity study of the Soviet republics fifty-five years later. That the Soviet-period series, extrapolated backwards over half a century of war, collectivisation and forced industrialisation, arrives within 3.5 per cent of an independently measured level in every year, and within 2 per cent in three of the four, is the strongest evidence available that the net error of the extrapolation is small. The monetary aggregates that an expenditure or income estimate would require are the figures that cannot be trusted: the Material Product System measured net material product at administered prices, excluded most services, double-counted intermediate transactions in its gross-output measures and, above all, understated inflation, so that official constant-price growth was too high; in Maddison's verdict, the official series `overstated growth, and understated inflation' \parencite[307]{Maddison1998b}. The Western response, begun by Bergson in the 1950s and institutionalised by the CIA from the 1960s, was to rebuild Soviet GNP from the bottom up, re-pricing output at factor cost, imputing the missing services and replacing the official value indices with indices built from physical output series weighted by value-added \parencite{bergson1950,bergson1961,cia1982a}. The CIA estimates were attacked from both sides, by critics who held that they overstated Soviet growth by ignoring deteriorating quality, over-reporting and hidden inflation, and faulted even the physical series as `open' statistics compiled for external consumption, and by a minority who contended that military output, housing and services were under-measured \parencite{assessingCIA1988,becker1994,schroeder1995}; Khanin's alternative statistics, as \textcite[144, 159]{harrison1993} showed, coincided with the CIA's for 1950--87. The assessments of Becker and Schroeder, the review by Maddison and the survey by Vonyó and Markevich all conclude that the CIA series contain errors in both directions, that most of the criticism `was not well founded', and that the physical-output method remains the best basis for measuring Soviet growth; the CIA's reworked series at 1982 prices \parencite{cia1990} is the one that entered the Maddison Project Database \parencites[309]{Maddison1998b}[279--80]{vonyoinmorys2021}. Ponomarenko's archival reconstruction of Russian national accounts reaches the same judgement from inside the Soviet statistical system: the physical output data `are apparently of high quality and can be used', whereas the official value indices were inflated by the pricing of new products \parencite[16--18, 73--4]{ponomarenko2002}. The literature on the Soviet economy has grown rapidly since the opening of the archives \parencite{zhuravskaya2024}, but its quantitative core for the post-war decades still rests on physical output series of this kind, and the non-Russian republics remain almost entirely without modern national accounts \parencite{kukic_soviet,voskoboynikov2021}. The series presented here follows this tradition and the procedure used for Lithuania and Estonia \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. A benchmark estimate of GDP is extrapolated with constant-price indices of sectoral value-added, each sector weighted by its share of GDP in the benchmark year: \[ \mathit{GDP}_{t} = \mathit{GDP}_{\mathrm{bench}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i}\, I_{it}, \] where $w_i$ is sector $i$'s share of benchmark GDP and $I_{it}$ its volume index in year $t$. The indices track gross output, inputs or employment and are combined with value-added weights, the procedure often loosely called single deflation; it is the `next best' procedure to double deflation where intermediate inputs cannot be observed \parencite[427--8, 444]{thomasfeinstein2003}, and the CIA itself double-deflated only agriculture \parencite[45]{cia1982a}. It matters, therefore, which Soviet data are used and which avoided. The distortions documented in the literature were concentrated in value aggregates, in the national income and gross output indices at `comparable prices', in the reporting of hidden price increases as real growth and in the double counting of the material product system \parencites[307]{Maddison1998b}{vonyo2017}[165]{mertelsmann_2003_there}; Khanin's own classification, as Harrison summarises it, is that `the ease of distortion remained greater for value series than for physical volumes', and that distortion was concentrated in heterogeneous products such as machinery and construction, while series for grain, milk, cement, electricity or freight are comparatively reliable \parencite[144, 152]{harrison1993}. The two diverge widely: the official Soviet index of Latvian industrial output at constant prices rises between 1940 and 1990 by several times the increase recorded by the physical-product index compiled here (Table~\ref{tab:sectoral}). The official index also values its 1940 base at an arbitrary lat--rouble parity that undervalued the last pre-Soviet year several-fold (Misiunas and Taagepera suspected in addition that only the five months of Soviet rule were counted; Mertelsmann finds for Estonia that the whole year was); its claim that industry had surpassed 1940 by 1947 is contradicted by the physical series \parencites[109]{years_of_dependence}[167]{mertelsmann_2003_there}[234]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}. The indices below rest almost entirely on physical quantities, on employment and on inputs; the one place where value data at comparable prices enter, trade turnover, is flagged and its bias bounded in the sensitivity analysis. \subsection{The 1990 benchmark} The Soviet-period series is anchored to Bolotin's estimate of the GDP of the Latvian SSR in 1990, the first systematic attempt to express the accounts of all fifteen republics in international dollars \parencite[181--92]{bolotin1992}. Military production, organised through all-Union enterprises and never reported at the republican level, is not captured, and Latvia hosted more of it than its neighbours: the VEF electrotechnical works, the Riga radio and instrument plants and the shipyards all carried `special' production for the Soviet armed forces \parencites[59--61]{upmalis_2015_latvijas}[74--5]{blaubergs_2015_vef}[103--4]{wbtransitionlatv}; the size of the Soviet garrison is likewise unknown between 1941 and 1989 and is treated as a source of bias below. Third, the year 1944 proved beyond reconstruction from Latvian sources, so that sectoral movements for 1943--5 are taken from the ratios observed in Lithuania, where documentation is better. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T2_sources.tex} \input{../../Tables/latvia/T2b_products.tex} \textit{Agriculture, forestry and fishing.} The index combines physical output of nine to ten crop categories and seven to sixteen animal products with timber removals and the fish catch, each sub-index weighted by its 1990 value-added, the crop and livestock weights coming from the World Bank's 1993 study and the split within grains from the Eurostat agricultural accounts \parencite[286]{wbtransitionlatv}. Early post-war output comes from unpublished returns on sown areas; yields for 1941--9 are obtained from animal numbers and the yields per animal of 1940, 1945 and 1950; disaggregated grain data for 1947--52 are not available, so that the grain categories move with the total. \textit{Industry.} Physical output series could be assembled for 129 products in ten of the eleven branches of the benchmark, electricity, fuels, metals, chemicals, machine-building and metal-working, wood and paper, building materials, light industry, food and a residual; the eleventh, petroleum refining, did not exist in Latvia (Table~\ref{tab:products}). The fuel index for 1980--90 is taken from the World Bank's study and extended with peat and natural gas; where a product series begins or ends with zero, production is assumed absent in the adjacent years. The branches are combined with the branch structure of the 1990 benchmark. For the interwar years the published manufacturing volume index for 1930--9 is used and the earlier years rest on employment adjusted for real wages, as in the Lithuanian and Estonian series \parencite[39, 45]{ostlandinzahlen}. \textit{Construction.} The Soviet-period index is a weighted index of the material inputs into construction, with weights from the 1987 input--output table, which is the CIA's procedure \parencite[66--89]{wbinputoutput1987}. \textit{Transport and communications.} Freight tonne-kilometres and passenger-kilometres across all modes are combined with a communications index built from postal and telegraph traffic, long-distance calls and radio and television sets in use, with weights from the 1987 input--output study. The years 1945--50 come from the Russian State Archive of the Economy; for 1941--4 no transport data exist and the sector is assumed to move with the rest of the economy; after 1990 the index follows sectoral employment. \textit{Trade, finance and housing.} Under planning industrial products circulated by allocation rather than through markets, so that the marketed-share approach of the interwar series cannot be used. The Soviet-period trade index instead chains the retail and wholesale turnover indices at comparable prices compiled by the Soviet statistical offices, the early post-war years coming from the USSR domestic-trade compendia; these are the only value series in the reconstruction. Finance and insurance follow employment, adjusted for productivity with the ratio of trade turnover to trade employment, as the CIA did; housing follows the housing stock derived from construction and population \parencites[319]{Maddison1998b}[49]{cia1982a}. \textit{Public and other services.} Public administration, health, education and science follow employment by branch, as in the CIA's accounts, with gaps in 1941--4, 1946--9 and 1951--4 interpolated. Defence is the least secure component. The Soviet garrison admitted under the mutual-assistance pact of October 1939 numbered about 30,000 \parencite[15--16]{years_of_dependence}, and some 80,000 Soviet troops were stationed in Latvia in 1990, far more in proportion to population than in Lithuania or Estonia; between those dates the garrison is interpolated between the 1940 and 1990 totals in step with public-administration employment, and after 1990 the index follows the withdrawal schedule and the formation of the Latvian forces. \textit{The war years.} Latvia was under German civil administration from 1941 to 1944, and the \textit{Reichskommissariat Ostland} published statistics, the \textit{Statistische Berichte für das Ostland} of 1942--4 and \textit{Ostland in Zahlen}, that cover crops, livestock, industrial output and employment but little else. Where these fail, the service sectors are interpolated between 1940 and the first post-war observation, and the movement between 1943 and 1945 is taken from the Lithuanian ratios. The estimates for 1941--5 are therefore `rough' in Feinstein's sense, with a margin of 15--25 per cent, and the 1944 trough is an order of magnitude rather than a measurement \parencite[21]{feinstein1972}. Because the Soviet-period series is extrapolated backwards through the war, an error in the wartime linkage would shift its level in 1937--40, so that the overlap tests the linkage together with the rest of the extrapolation; the spliced series, which follows the interwar series to 1940, is affected only through the 1940 average. \subsection{Population and borders} Latvia's borders changed once, when the eastern Abrene district was transferred to the Russian republic in 1944. The series to 1944 refer to the borders of the republic and the series from 1945 to present-day borders. This is the convention of the Maddison Project, which treats income per head as unaffected by a territorial change that moves less than a third of the population \parencites[629]{maddison_project_paper2014}[30]{bolt_zanden_newgdp2021}; the transferred district held a few per cent of the pre-war population at most \parencites[74]{years_of_dependence}[129--30]{hiden_salmon}, and was rural and poorer than the national average, so that the break in income per head is small and no adjustment has been made. The population series rests on the censuses of 1920, 1925, 1930, 1935, 1959, 1970, 1979 and 1989 and the year-end estimates of the Latvian statistical office and the `Baltic 100' database, with mid-year figures as the average of consecutive year-ends; wartime losses, the flight of some 120,000 ethnic Latvians to the West in 1944 \parencite[86]{king_1965_economic}, the Holocaust and the deportations are taken from the demographic literature, and the Soviet garrison of 1940--1 is added to the resident population. Between 1939 and 1945 the resident population fell by \lvPOPchangeWARtwo{} per cent, of which a small part, of the order of two points, reflects the border change (Table~\ref{tab:series}). \subsection{The interwar series and its extension to 1919 and 1940} The interwar series is that of \textcite{Klimantas2024}, which extrapolates the 1935 benchmark of \textcite{norkuslatvia1935} to 1920--39 with sectoral volume indices built from the publications of the Latvian statistical office;\footnote{Bukowski, Kowalski and Wroński object that this extrapolation holds relative prices fixed at their 1935 structure although agricultural--industrial relative prices fluctuated between the wars \parencite[6]{bukowski_2026_economic}; the objection is the index-number problem discussed under sensitivity below.} the benchmark itself was converted into international dollars by a bilateral price comparison with Sweden of the kind used for Lithuania in 1937 and Estonia in 1938. Two years are added here. For 1919, the first year of the republic's existence, the crop, livestock, railway and employment series were carried back with the data for 1919 where they exist and with 1920 ratios where they do not; forestry, fishing, finance and the household services follow the population or the sectors to which they are tied. For 1940, the year of the Soviet occupation, the 1940 yearbook, the Ostland publications and the first Soviet returns provide output and employment for most sectors, imports are assumed equal to their deflated 1939 value, and defence includes the Soviet garrison. The resulting figure for 1919, \lv{1919}~\intlnineteen{}, is 37 per cent below the 1913 benchmark of Norkus and Markevičiūtė, and makes Latvia, with Lithuania, the most devastated economy in Europe at the end of the First World War, as contemporaries and later historians have judged it \parencites[322--3]{norkusdvides}[44]{krumins_2024_makroekonomiska}. \subsection{Aggregation, splicing and the overlaps} Each of the two new series is compiled in constant benchmark-year prices and expressed in \intlnineteen{} through its benchmark. The interwar series covers 1919--40 and the Soviet-period series 1937--95, so that the two overlap for four years; the Soviet-period series in turn overlaps for six years with a modern series obtained by backcasting the Maddison Project's 2011 benchmark with the World Bank's constant-price growth rates of GDP per capita, which are used in preference to the Maddison Project's own 1990--2010 growth for reasons given below \parencite{mpd2023,wdi2024}. Table~\ref{tab:overlaps} reports the overlaps. \input{../../Tables/latvia/T3_overlaps.tex} In 1937--40 the two series differ by $+$1.7, $+$3.2, $-$1.9 and $-$0.7 per cent, all within the 5 per cent margin that Feinstein reserved for `firm' estimates, and not of one sign. The test is demanding. The two series share no sources, the one resting on the republic's own statistics and the other on Soviet yearbooks and post-war archives; no weights, one using the structure of 1935 and the other that of 1990; and no benchmark, one a bilateral price comparison with Sweden, the other a purchasing-power-parity study of the Soviet republics fifty-five years later. That the Soviet-period series, extrapolated backwards over half a century of war, collectivisation and forced industrialisation, arrives within 3.5 per cent of an independently measured level in every year, and within 2 per cent in three of the four, is the strongest evidence available that the net error of the extrapolation is small. It cannot exclude errors that happen to offset, but the two index-number biases discussed below, late base-year weights and fixed value-added weights, would both understate growth and so would both place the backcast 1937--40 level above the interwar series; a net understatement of as little as 0.1 percentage point a year over 1940--90 would place it 5 per cent above in every overlap year, which is not observed. \textcite[323--6]{broad2007} regarded time-series projections as consistent with direct benchmarks when they agree within 10 per cent; the Latvian overlap meets that standard in each of four consecutive years, as the Lithuanian and Estonian series do in 1939--40 and 1937--40 \parencite{klimantas2026soviet,klimantas2025estonia}. The two series are spliced at 1940 by taking the average of the two estimates for that year, which moves the 1940 figure by less than half a per cent. The second overlap validates the benchmark. In 1990 the Soviet-period series stands 2.9 per cent below the modern series and in 1991 \ovd{1991} per cent above it: Bolotin's purchasing-power parities and the Maddison Project's 2011 ICP round, carried backwards with the national accounts, are two routes that share no data and arrive at the same level within 3 per cent. The series are spliced at 1991, the year of restored independence, by averaging. Thereafter the gap widens to \ovd{1992} per cent in 1992 before narrowing to \ovd{1995} per cent by 1995, because the Soviet-period series continues to value the collapse of Soviet-era output at 1990 weights and misses the new activities, above all in services, that were emerging unrecorded \parencite[260]{kyn_1997_eastern}, while the modern series, like Hamilton and de Vries's recent extrapolation of the post-Soviet republics from mid-1990s benchmarks, carries the weights of the surviving branches backwards and records a shallower decline \parencites[11]{imf_transition}[17]{hamilton_transition}. The two bracket the true fall; the modern series is preferred from 1992. It is anchored on the Maddison Project's 2011 figure for Latvia and carried back with World Bank growth because the Maddison Project's own path for 1990--2010 implies far slower growth than the national accounts record, so that its 1990 level, 15,806~\intltwenty{} or 9,916~\intlnineteen{}, stands \mpdgap{1990} per cent above Bolotin's independent estimate; since the two share the 2011 anchor, the whole of that difference lies in the growth attributed to the 1990s, not in the level \parencite{mpd2023,wdi2024}. \subsection{The final series and earlier estimates} The 1913 figure is the benchmark of \textcite[603]{norkusmark2021}, taken as published; there are no estimates for 1914--18. The Maddison Project's Latvian levels for 1973--85, carried back from a 1990 level with net material product growth, lie 3--8 per cent \textit{below} the new series, whereas its 1989 level lies \mpdgap{1989} per cent above it and its 1990 level \mpdgap{1990} per cent above: the Maddison Project records Latvian income per head rising by 5 per cent in 1989 and again in 1990, when every physical indicator compiled here was already falling; the EBRD's index of real GDP likewise rises by 6.8 per cent in 1989 and 2.9 per cent in 1990, whereas Krūmiņš's physical series put 1990 output below that of 1985 \parencites[269]{kyn_1997_eastern}[348--50]{krumins_2017_gorbacova}. The first is the index-number problem of a single late benchmark. A late base assigns to each sector the relative prices of the end of the period, and since the sectors that grew fastest were those whose relative prices fell, late weights understate growth; this is the effect that Gerschenkron showed for Soviet machinery, when Bergson's GNP for 1928--37 grows by 175 per cent at 1928 prices and by 62 per cent at 1937 prices \parencites[453]{gerschenkron1957}[517]{feinsteinthomas2002}. It is far smaller here. The effect is concentrated in the early phases of industrialisation \parencite[85]{jonassardy1970}, and for the post-war Soviet economy it is modest: the CIA's move from 1970 to 1982 prices lowered measured growth over 1951--84 by about half a point a year \parencites[8]{cia1990}[156]{harrison1993}. The bound comes from the data: if 1990 weights understated Latvian growth over 1940--90, the Soviet-period series would arrive in 1937--40 systematically above the 1935-weighted interwar series, and it does not. And the procedure is that of every comparable reconstruction, the CIA's 1982 weights for 1950--90 among them, in which Maddison found `nothing untoward' \parencite[312]{Maddison1998b}. The second is the fixed ratio of value-added to gross output. Thomas and Feinstein's simulations found that the procedure understated value-added growth by between 0.15 and 1 percentage point a year; the Swedish accounts, which allow single- and double-deflated series to be compared, show an understatement of the deflator of 17 per cent over the three-quarters of a century after 1875 \parencites[19]{swedengdp_15602010}[148--53]{lobellschonkrantz2008}, and the bound in Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}, 14 per cent over the half-century, is in the lower part of that range, as befits indices that track output product by product and an economy that adhered to mass-production methods throughout its existence \parencite[195--7]{berend_centraleastern19441993}. The sign of the bias depends on the movement of input relative to output prices, and the Swedish figure is taken as a bound on its magnitude rather than as evidence of its direction in a planned economy. The error accumulates over the extrapolation and is largest in the earliest years of the Soviet-period series, precisely where the overlap shows the series within 3.5 per cent of an independent level. On 25 March and the days following, more than 40,000 people, most of them farming families, were sent east;\footnote{Feest's count is 41,445 \parencite[99--100]{feest2014}; for the date see \parencites[172]{strods_2006_nonviolent}[75]{pocius_2019_lietuvos}; the older Western literature put the number at 50,000 or more \parencites[90]{labsvirs_1959_case}[99]{years_of_dependence}.} the share of farms collectivised rose from a tenth at the beginning of 1949 to 85 per cent a year later on the count used in Table~\ref{tab:collectivisation}, and to 93 per cent by the end of December 1949 on Krūmiņš's,\footnote{Misiunas and Taagepera also give 93 per cent at the end of 1949 \parencite[102]{years_of_dependence}; Terleckas gives 90 per cent on 1 January 1950 \parencite[225]{terleckas_2026_siferio}.} and the cooperative dairies and credit societies of the interwar republic, already dismantled, were replaced by procurement prices that fell for meat from 16,640 to 680 roubles a tonne \parencites[245--50]{krumins_2017_sovetizacijas}[86--99]{labsvirs_1959_case}[48]{aizsilnieks_1974_sovietization}. Agricultural output, 59 per cent of its 1938 level in 1947, fluctuated between 60 and 67 per cent of it through 1955; grain yields in the early 1950s were little more than half those of the late 1930s, and milk output less than half; the sector regained its pre-war level only in \sregain{Primary}, crops in \sregain{Crops} and livestock in \sregain{Livestock}, and the kolkhoz households' private plots, a tenth of the sown area, supplied more than half of the meat and milk sold in the cities into the late 1950s \parencites[219--23, 269--71]{labsvirs_1959_case}[281--4]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1950}. The two decades to 1968 were the fastest the Latvian economy had yet recorded. Industrial output grew by \sgr{Industry}{1950}{1968} per cent a year, heavy industry by \sgr{Heavy}{1948}{1969} per cent a year over 1948--69, construction by \sgr{Construction}{1950}{1968} per cent and transport by \sgr{Transport}{1950}{1968}; total GDP grew by \tgr{1950}{1968} per cent a year and income per head by \gr{1950}{1968}. The growth was extensive in the Soviet sense, carried by machine-building for the Union market, by the electric trains, radios and telephone equipment of Riga and by a second wave of chemical and fibre plants in the 1960s, and by labour: a net 292,000 immigrants arrived between 1960 and 1985, and Latvians fell from 62 per cent of the population in 1959 to 52 per cent in 1989 \parencites[303]{krumins_2017_tautsaimnieciba_1960}[50]{eglite_2015_migracija}[43--4]{puur_2019_turbulent}.
